extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners; corporate communications and management professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and conceptual criteria for how public relations practitioners and organizations should define, evaluate, and enact responsibility to publics, including appropriate communication models, categories of responsibilities, sample measures, and practical contributions of PR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of PR model
rubrics_metrics.description: At times, one organization will find that a different model works best for different problems or for different public relations activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are four models (press agentry/publicity, public information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric). Research on conditions favoring each model has only begun, so practitioners should recognize that the same principles will not work all the time and choose models according to problem type and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the two-way symmetric model for social responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A large, regulated business firm will want to use the two-way symmetric model to help maintain the social responsibility its government regulators require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balanced, two-way communication provides the most effective mechanism for an organization to evaluate its social responsibility. The two-way symmetric model often replaces other models under pressure for public responsibility, though other models can sometimes promote responsibility under constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: No license for irresponsibility across models
rubrics_metrics.description: In none of the models does the practitioner have a license for irresponsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regardless of which PR model is used, practitioners must not act irresponsibly. Public responsibility is a core article in professional public relations codes of ethics; ethical constraints apply even when using press agentry, public information, or two-way asymmetric approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not persuade publics to their harm
rubrics_metrics.description: The press agent/publicist or the two-way asymmetric practitioner should not attempt to persuade members of publics to do something that could harm them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using public-information approaches, practitioners should report what the organization has done to be responsible and explain lapses into irresponsibility. Examples (Firestone, Ford Pinto, Allied Chemical) illustrate damage when full information about product dangers was not provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'public responsibility' over 'social responsibility'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the term 'public responsibility' rather than 'social responsibility' because organizations can identify consequences on publics more easily than on society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public responsibility focuses the organization's responsibilities on primary and secondary involvements (consequences on publics) rather than the infinite boundary implied by 'social responsibility.' This helps managers set clearer limits on organizational responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three categories of organizational responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational responsibilities can be categorized as: (1) performance of the organization's basic tasks; (2) concern with consequences of those activities on groups outside the organization; (3) concern with helping to solve general social problems not connected to the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers should determine which category (or mix) the organization will emphasize. Preston and Post argue the organization should be responsible primarily for the first two categories (primary and secondary involvements) and not necessarily for broad social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public perception determines responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Publics ultimately decide whether organizations have been responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations professionals must help the organization realize when publics believe it is behaving irresponsibly and suggest how the organization can be responsive; they must also help publics understand organizational behavior so judgments are based on knowledge rather than hearsay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons to be responsible: altruism and self-interest (avoid regulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments for being socially responsible include altruism (obligation to serve society) and self-interest: publics that view organizations as irresponsible turn to government for regulation, which imposes costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicating responsibility helps maintain organizational freedom to operate and avoid increasingly restrictive environments; a strong communications link with publics and government is necessary to preserve favorable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preston and Post: interpenetrating systems theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations and systems in their environment are 'interpenetrating systems' — neither completely controlling nor controlled by the social environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public responsibility results from communication, negotiation, and compromise between interpenetrating systems. This theory implies that organizations will adopt different PR models depending on whether they try to control or adapt to other systems (press agentry/asymmetric reflect attempts to control; two-way symmetric/public information reflect negotiation/adaptation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalog of corporate social responsibilities (student list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students reviewed twelve representative books and constructed a list of sixty-four business social responsibilities grouped into categories such as ecology and environmental quality, consumerism, community needs, governmental relations, business contributions, economic activities, minorities and disadvantaged persons, labor relations, stockholder relations, communication, and research and development for national needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comprehensive catalog can be used by PR managers to identify candidate responsibilities for their organizations and to decide which responsibilities to advocate to management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Impact (Johnston category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic Impact: number of new jobs created by type and location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of Johnston's sample measures — organizations can measure and report their local economic contributions as an accountability metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of Products (Johnston category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of Products: number and type of product liability complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product quality metrics (complaints, recalls, defects) are a direct measure of responsibility for primary organizational outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer Relations (Johnston category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer Relations: number of complaints, by type; turnaround time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure responsiveness to consumer issues (complaint volume, resolution speed) as an indicator of public responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental Impacts (Johnston category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Environmental Impacts: level of emissions, by type of pollutant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify pollutant emissions and other environmental performance measures to assess responsibility for environmental consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy Conservation (Johnston category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Energy Conservation: amounts of energy conserved, by major type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report energy savings and conservation measures as part of environmental responsibility reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee Relations — Equal Employment (Johnston submeasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employee Relations: Equal employment: number of minorities and women employed in nine categories defined by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standardized EEO categories to measure diversity and equal employment practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee Relations — Job Satisfaction (Johnston submeasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employee Relations: Job satisfaction: number of employees involved in career-advancement programs, or provision of day care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track participation in career development and family-support programs as indicators of concern for employee welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee Relations — Occupational Safety and Health (Johnston submeasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employee Relations: Occupational safety and health: number of accidents, by type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record accidents and safety incidents to monitor and report occupational safety performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investments with social impact (Johnston category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investments (primarily for banks and insurance companies): investments that have social impact and that may be risky and have below-normal rates of return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report and evaluate investments chosen for social impact, acknowledging potential trade-offs with returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community Relations — Voluntary Contributions (Johnston submeasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Community Relations: Voluntary contributions: assessment of impact of charitable contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the impact (not just dollar amount) of charitable giving on community outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community Relations — Minority Economic Development (Johnston submeasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Community Relations: Minority economic development: dollar amounts of goods and services purchased from minority-owned firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track procurement from minority-owned businesses as a measurable contribution to minority economic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community Relations — Other Activities (Johnston submeasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other Community Relations Activities: number and type of community activities held on company property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report community engagement activities hosted by the organization as part of community relations performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government Relations (Johnston category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government Relations: number and occupation of employees who have direct contact with government officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and report the extent and nature of direct government relations activities to provide transparency about lobbying and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which responsibilities to emphasize — managerial choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The question for managers is which responsibilities the organization should emphasize and which it can or should do; organizations cannot do all responsibilities equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers should use categories (basic tasks, consequences, general social problems) and stakeholder expectations (surveys, publics) to prioritize responsibilities and allocate PR advocacy accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR contribution: internal reporting to management
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations managers can communicate to organizational subsystems what publics believe to be irresponsible organizational behaviors and recommend structural and policy changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public responsibility must be a criterion applied to management decisions and reward systems; internal reporting enables fundamental changes in structure/policy when irresponsibility is detected (Preston and Post).

rubrics_metrics.name: PR contribution: reporting to publics and rectification
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations can report to publics what the organization has done that is responsible or irresponsible, and what it is doing to rectify areas of irresponsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent external communication helps publics make informed judgments and is a practical action PR can take when addressing public responsibility issues (e.g., Three-Mile Island, Love Canal, Nestlé cases).
